stories.headline: Update: Fed Holds Rates Steady as Inflation Hits 3-Year High Under New Chair Warsh
stories.summary:
The Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate steady Wednesday under new Chair Kevin Warsh, as inflation runs at more than twice the Fed's 2% target — its highest level in three years. All 12 members of the Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to hold rates at the current level between 3.5% and 4%, though nine members signaled they expect a rate hike before year's end, a significant shift from projections issued three months earlier.

Warsh, Trump's nominee who recently replaced former Chair Jerome Powell, used his first post-decision press conference to pledge a commitment to price stability. 'Persistently high prices are a burden for the American people,' Warsh told reporters in Washington. 'This committee will deliver price stability.' The FOMC statement cited supply shocks, particularly in the energy sector driven by the Middle East conflict, as a key driver of elevated prices.

The decision arrives days after the U.S. and Iran announced a deal — set to be formally signed Friday in Switzerland — that includes plans to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the maritime route through which roughly one-fifth of global oil supply passes. Oil prices fell to their lowest level since March following the announcement, and gasoline prices dipped below $4 a gallon for the first time since March, offering potential relief. However, grocery and energy prices remain well above pre-war levels.

Markets had widely anticipated the hold, but the hawkish tilt among committee members — with four in ten odds now assigned to a December rate hike by the CME FedWatch Tool — represents a concrete new development. The rate decision is the first major policy action under Warsh's leadership and will be closely watched as a signal of how the new Fed chair intends to balance inflation control against economic growth risks.

stories.headline: Update: Speaker Johnson Says Congress Will Not Lead on AI Safety Regulation
stories.summary:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) declared Sunday that Congress will not take the lead on regulating artificial intelligence safety, even as calls for federal action intensified following warnings from AI insiders about existential risks. Johnson made the remarks during an appearance on CNN's 'State of the Union,' rejecting calls from fellow House members to cancel recess and return to Washington to pass emergency AI safeguard legislation.

The announcement is a significant development in the rapidly escalating AI safety debate. This past week, the four largest AI laboratories endorsed slowing development of their most advanced models, and a bipartisan group of House members urged Johnson to convene an emergency session to legislate guardrails. Johnson's refusal effectively shelves any near-term congressional action and leaves AI oversight to existing executive-branch agencies and voluntary industry commitments.

Supporters of Johnson's position argue that Congress lacks the technical expertise to legislate AI effectively and that heavy-handed regulation could stifle American innovation and cede ground to China. Critics, including Democrats and some Republicans, counter that voluntary measures are insufficient given the pace of AI advancement and the severity of risks described by the industry's own executives.

Johnson also addressed President Trump's proposal to send $5,000 dividend checks to adult U.S. citizens, saying the plan would require congressional approval — contradicting claims by Trump and his aides that the executive branch could act unilaterally on a disbursement that could exceed $1.3 trillion.

stories.headline: Republicans Elevate Anti-Muslim Rhetoric as Midterm Strategy, Drawing Bipartisan Criticism
stories.summary:
Republican leaders amplified anti-Muslim messaging at the party's first-ever midterm convention in Dallas this past week, targeting prominent Muslim Democratic figures — including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed — as central villains in the party's closing midterm pitch. Senior GOP figures, including Sen. Ted Cruz, framed Muslim Democrats as a core threat, a line of attack that has intensified as midterm elections approach in seven weeks.

Democrats and a number of political observers condemned the rhetoric as dangerous and discriminatory, arguing it conflates religion with political allegiance and risks inciting harassment or violence against Muslim Americans. The attacks have drawn particular scrutiny given that Mamdani, New York's first Muslim mayor, was already the subject of a petition from 9/11 victims' families over his attendance at the anniversary ceremony.

Republicans defending the strategy argue the attacks are policy-based rather than religious, pointing to Mamdani's and El-Sayed's positions on immigration, foreign policy, and social issues. They contend that Democratic candidates in deep-blue cities and competitive Senate states represent a sharp leftward shift that Republicans need to make vivid to motivate their base before November.

The controversy underscores the increasingly sharp identity-politics framing on both sides of the midterm battle, with Republicans betting that cultural and demographic contrasts will drive turnout in an environment of elevated inflation and continued Middle East conflict. Analysts note that the strategy carries risk, potentially alienating moderate suburban voters even as it energizes the GOP base.

stories.headline: Uganda's King Oyo Buried Amid Succession Dispute and Family's Claims of House Arrest
stories.summary:
Uganda's King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, once recognized by Guinness World Records as the world's youngest reigning monarch, was buried Saturday in Fort Portal following a private ceremony, as thousands of mourners lined the streets to pay respects. Oyo, 34, had ruled the traditional kingdom of Tooro in western Uganda since the age of three and died last month while undergoing cancer treatment in the United States.

The burial took place against the backdrop of a contested succession. Clan elders named TV news presenter Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, 56 — a cousin of the late king — as the next monarch, with Kijanangoma performing the ritual of casting nine coffee beans into Oyo's grave, symbolizing the transition of power. However, Oyo's family has rejected that choice, with his sister Princess Ruth Komuntale stating the late king left a 2022 will naming his young son as successor, though the boy's identity has not been disclosed.

Oyo's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, alleged that royal guards had been withdrawn from the palace and replaced by soldiers, effectively placing the royal family under house arrest and restricting their ability to receive visitors. The clan overseeing succession denied any irregularity, with clan head Omusuuga Charles Karumasi stating all procedures followed Tooro cultural tradition.

Uganda's Archbishop Stephen Kazimba Mugalu and President Yoweri Museveni both called for unity and peaceful resolution of the dispute. Tooro is one of several traditional Ugandan kingdoms abolished in 1967 and restored in the 1990s under Museveni; their monarchs hold cultural rather than political authority, but succession disputes can carry significant social weight in the region.

stories.headline: Federal Judge Rules Trump's Plan to Halve FEMA Workforce Illegal
stories.summary:
A federal judge ruled Friday that the Trump administration acted unlawfully when it directed the Department of Homeland Security to cut the Federal Emergency Management Agency's workforce in half. U.S. District Judge Susan Illston of the Northern District of California found that DHS "unlawfully usurped the authority" of FEMA in attempting to implement the cuts, and issued an order blocking the directive from taking effect.

The ruling came during an active hurricane season, with the judge explicitly noting that the workforce reductions would hinder FEMA's ability to respond to disasters. The administration had argued the restructuring was within executive authority over agency operations.

Critics of the plan, including Democrats and emergency management professionals, said gutting FEMA's staff during hurricane season created unacceptable risks for Americans in disaster-prone areas. Supporters of the administration's broader government-reduction agenda contend that federal agencies are overstaffed and that leaner operations can remain effective. The ruling is the latest in a series of court setbacks for the administration's efforts to dramatically reduce the federal workforce.

stories.headline: Update: Murder Arrest Made in Death of Tasia Fortune, Black Woman Found Hanging in Mississippi
stories.summary:
Mississippi police arrested 51-year-old Jarques Ratliff, a Black Jackson resident, on a murder charge Friday in connection with the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in the backyard of an abandoned Jackson home on August 3. The arrest followed Thursday's determination by the state medical examiner that Fortune's death was a homicide, which enabled police to execute warrants they already had prepared.

Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney described the arrest as "an important development" but emphasized the investigation remains active and additional arrests are expected. Ratliff had an "association" with Fortune, police said, though they declined to elaborate on the nature of their relationship. It was not immediately determined whether Ratliff had legal representation.

Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey, said she burst into tears upon learning of the arrest, telling officers "thank you, thank you, thank you," while acknowledging the family still lacks answers about motive. The case drew intense national and international media attention after Fortune's loved ones insisted she would not have taken her own life. The homicide ruling and subsequent arrest resolve the initial uncertainty about the manner of death that had fueled public concern.

stories.headline: Wisconsin GOP Gubernatorial Candidate Tom Tiffany Survives Emergency Plane Landing in Lake
stories.summary:
Wisconsin Republican gubernatorial candidate and U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and a pilot escaped with minor injuries Saturday night after their small four-seat Bonanza aircraft lost power on approach to Wausau Downtown Airport and made an emergency water landing in Lake Wausau. Tiffany said the incident occurred following his appearance at a La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner.

After the plane hit the water, it began filling and sinking before emergency responders could reach them, forcing both Tiffany and the pilot to exit the aircraft and swim to a shallow area. Rescue crews from the Wausau Fire Department reached them by boat, and both were transported to Aspirus Wausau Hospital with only minor injuries.

"God was watching over us tonight," Tiffany wrote on social media, expressing gratitude to first responders and noting his wife Chris was at his bedside. The incident drew an outpouring of well-wishes on social media. Tiffany, who represents Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District, is running as the Trump-backed Republican candidate for governor against likely Democratic nominee Francesca Hong.

stories.headline: Céline Dion Returns to Stage in Paris for First Full Concert in Six Years
stories.summary:
Canadian singer Céline Dion performed her first full concert in six years Saturday in Paris, opening a sold-out residency at a Paris venue after a prolonged battle with stiff-person syndrome, a rare neurological disorder that had sidelined her career. The residency is scheduled to run for 26 concerts over the next eight months.

Fans began gathering outside her hotel as early as 6 a.m. to catch a glimpse of the performer before she departed for the show. Dion is one of the best-selling music artists of all time, and her return has been widely anticipated by fans around the world who followed her public struggle with the debilitating condition.

The Paris residency marks a significant milestone in what has been described as a difficult personal and professional recovery. Dion had previously announced her comeback with the phrase "I'm so ready for this," and her appearance Saturday was seen as confirmation that she had regained the health necessary to resume performing at the highest level.
